headline: Waived waiving of Water Works building permit fees, instead creating a dedicated fund, and added staff across several departments.
summary: The board heard extensive public comment on the Nickenley Turenne police shooting, the five-day return-to-duty policy, and ICE cooperation, then voted to maintain the Manchester Police Department's existing federal law enforcement practices rather than seek 287(g) deputization. It approved numerous consent agenda items, resolutions, and bond authorizations for FY2027 capital projects, added positions in Water Works, Assessors, Tax Collector, and Solicitor offices, and reversed a committee decision on waiving Water Works building permit fees.
decisions: Took public comments under advisement and agreed to file any written documentation submitted.
Approved the consent agenda, including minutes, donations, sidewalk petitions, committee recommendations, and confirmations.

Approved the Oral Health Program funding amendment of $23,605.99.
Approved the Canal St Multi-Modal Trail (TAP 4) funding transfer of $1,100,000.
Approved the Fire Chief's request to apply for a $337,399 Assistance to Firefighters Grant.
Approved extending the Independent City Auditor CIP to September 1, 2026.
Approved extending the Dilapidated Building Demolition CIP to June 30, 2027.

Confirmed nominations to the Board of Health, Conservation Commission, Heritage Commission, Planning Board, and Safety Review Board.

Enrolled four Community Improvement Program resolutions totaling over $1.1 million.
Approved and laid over the $27,000 Women's Locker Room Expansion bond resolution.
Approved converting one Customer Service Representative III position from part-time to full-time in the Assessors' Office.
Approved integrating the Parking Division into the Police Department's organizational structure.
Bifurcated the Tax Collector's staffing and hours request into two separate votes.
Approved adding two Municipal Revenue Clerk positions to the Tax Collector's department.

Enrolled the remaining bond resolutions for FY2027 capital projects.
Ordained the ordinance amendment creating the Assistant Water Works Director position.
Voted to support the Manchester Police Department's existing arrangement with federal law enforcement rather than pursue ICE deputization.

BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
August 4, 2026 at 7:00 PM 
 
Mayor Ruais called the meeting to order. 
 
The Clerk called the roll. 
 
Present: Aldermen Kaw-uh, Goonan, Dexter, Fajardo, Bonilla, Kantor, Trisciani, 
  O’Neil, Terrio, Sapienza, Burkush, Barry, Vincent, Thomas 
 
Mayor Ruais: With t he board's indulgence, I have two proclamations tonight . Will the 
members of the Manchester Fire Department who are with us here this evening  please 
come forward ? L adies and gentlemen, it is truly an honor and a privilege tonight to 
recognize the heroic actions of th e Manchester Fire Department during the incident that 
occurred on Wednesday, June 24th. City of Manchester, a Resolution: Whereas at 
approximately 1:25 a.m. on Wednesday, June 24th, 2026, Manchester Fire Department 
personnel responded to a reported motorcycle crash on I-293 northbound at exit five near 
Granite Street, where Adam Brackett, Tyler Stratton, Chad Gamache and Ken Wong 
located an unoccupied motorcycle and quickly discovered the approximately 65ft below 
on the shoreline of the Merrimack River. And  whereas, Robert Plantier assumed 
command of the incident, while Valerie Mathis, Don Pullen, and Julian Rizzuto 
coordinated additional resources, dispatching Thomas Burk ush, Jason Coulter, Aaron 
Pascalis, Jared Pellerin, Chris Ellison, Jonathan Goldrick, T heodore Partington, Steve 
Goupil, Hannah Guerrero, Brianna Gaskill and Mary Wu to assist in the rescue operation. 
And whereas, because the victim could only be reached by water, Thomas Burk ush, 
Jason Coulter, Aaron Pascalis and Jared Pellerin rapidly reach ed the victim by boat, 
providing lifesaving care to stabilize the patient and return to the boat launch where 
Hannah Guerrero and Brianna Gaskill transported the patient to E lliot Hospital.  And 
whereas, the coordinated efforts and professionalism of Adam B rackett, Tyler Stratton, 
Chad Gamache, Ken Wong, Dan Boissonnault , Morgan Brennan, Cole Lodi, Chris 
Ellison, Jonathan Goldrick, Theodore Partington, Steve Goupil, Thomas Burks, Jason 
Coulter, Aaron Pascalis, Jared Pellerin, Robert Plantier, Valerie Mathis,  Don Pullen, 
Julian Rizzuto, Hannah Guerrero, Brianna Gaskill, and Mary Wu were instrumental in 
saving this victim's life. Now, therefore, I, Jay Ru ais, Mayor of the City of Manchester, 
New Hampshire, do hereby recognize and commend Adam Brackett, Tyler Stratton, Chad 
Gamache, Ken Wong, Dan Bossano, Morgan Brennan, Cole Lodi, Chris Ellison,
August 4, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 2 of 62 
 
Jonathan. Goldrick, Theodore Partington, Steve Goepel, Thomas Burk uss, Jason 
Coulter, Aaron Pascalis, Jared Pellerin, Robert Plantier, Valerie Mathis, Don Pullen, 
Julian Rizzuto, Hannah Guerrero, Brianna Gaskill and Mary Wu , for their outstanding 
professionalism, courage, teamwork and dedication to public service. Their swift and 
decisive actions during the June 24th, 2026 , rescue exemplified the highest traditions of 
emergency response and were instrumental in saving a life. On behalf of the City of 
Manchester and its residents, I extend my sincere gratitude and appreciation for their 
exceptional service and unwavering commitment to protecting our community. Thank you 
all very much. 
 
Mayor Ruais: And at this time, will the Public Health and Safety Team, the PHAST team, 
please come forward. City of Manchester, a Resolution: Whereas the Public Health and 
Safety Team was formed in 2022 with American Recovery Plan funding and partnership 
with the City of Manchester Health Department and the Manchester Police Department 
to provide highly trained, multicultural and multilingual community health workers to 
address neighborhood level concerns in all 12 city wards. And whereas in 2025, this team 
provided 1,272 residents with care coordination services, including home visits through 
2,096 unique encounters across the community, with a total of 1,082 referral connections 
to external service organizations. And whereas the CHWs help residents with food 
insecurity, transportation challenges, public assistance, enrollment, housing, navigation, 
medical and dental care linkages, and connections to financial and legal support while 
also completing Meals on Wheels , wellness checks, home visits for high risk expectant 
mothers, and community outreach with MPD’s critical response units for those who have 
recently overdosed. And whereas the CHWs have responded to many crisis situations 
involving residents experiencing domestic violence, loss of housing due to fires, risk of 
homelessness, severe medical complexity, or disability. And whereas several CHWs 
have dealt with life-or-death situations, including a recent wellness check for a vulnerable 
senior resident who could not be contacted, prompting the CHW to engage first 
responders who found the resident unresponsive on the floor and credit  the CHW with 
saving this individual's life. Now, therefore, I, Jay Ruais, Mayor of the City of Manchester, 
do hereby recognize and commend the Public H ealth and Safety Team for their 
exceptional service and dedication to the residents of Manchester and extend my sincere
August 4, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 3 of 62 
 
appreciation for their commitment to strengthening our community and improving the lives 
of those they serve. Thank you all deeply. 
 
PUBLIC COMMENT   
 
1. The Mayor advised that the purpose of the public comment session is to give 
residents of Manchester the opportunity to address the Board. All people wishing 
to speak must sign up with their name, address and topic. Once called, they will 
have up to three minutes to speak and any comments must be directed to the 
chair and concluded when their time is up. If the Clerk calls their name and they 
are not present to speak, they will not be given a second opportunity. Any 
resident wishing to speak will come forward to the nearest microphone, clearly 
state their name and address when recognized and give their comments.   
 
Troy Micklon, 29 Ode Way: I'm here tonight to briefly talk about two issues. First, I'd like 
to invite all ward nine residents to our community meeting, which will be held this 
Thursday, August 6th, at 6 p.m. at the Bishop O'Neill Youth Center located at 20 South 
Elm Street. These meetings are an opportunity for neighbors to come together, discuss 
issues affecting our community, and have open conversations about what's happening 
in ward nine. While the concerns involve rising taxes, public safety infrastructure or 
neighborhood quality of life issues, I encourage everyone to attend. I hope to see you 
there, Mr. Mayor, our current sitting ward alderman, and two aldermen at large. Second, 
I'd like to express my support for the demolition proceedings for the hazardous structure 
at 44 Benton Street in ward nine, which I believe is item 27 in your agenda. I've spoken 
with several neighborhood residents, including abutters on Brownell Ave, who shared 
years of frustration with this property. They've dealt with ongoing concerns, repeated 
trespassing, and the feeling that nothing was ever going to change. After reading 
tonight's agenda, it is clear this isn't a situation where the city is acting too quickly. 
According to the documentation in your packets, this property has been subject to code 
enforcement issues since 2021. There have been multiple notices of violations, 
citations, and repeated opportunities for the owner to correct the problems. Despite all 
that, the property remains unsafe, unsightly and unsecured, and continues to attract 
illegal activity. The Manchester Fire Department has also determined the property 
poses a hazard to neighboring homes and to first responders. No one wants to see a 
home demolished, but there comes a point where protecting the surrounding 
neighborhood has to take priority. I appreciate the work that the various city
August 4, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 4 of 62 
 
departments have put into this case over the past several years, and I encourage the 
board to move this petition forward so this long-standing problem can finally be 
resolved, and the property could eventually become an asset to the neighborhood 
instead of a liability. 
 
Austin Bouchard, Ward 2: There are votes that spend money. There are votes that alter 
policy, and there are rare votes that alter the moral relationship between a people and 
their government. The vote of June 9th was such a vote. What was broken that night was 
larger than the tax cap. A covenant was broken , the understanding that public power is 
borrowed, that promises bind those who make them, and that government exists by the 
consent of the governed. Many members of this board, including the mayor, sought office 
promising to respect the tax cap. Yet when principle first carried a price, only two kept 
faith throughout. There are only two possible judgments. Either those promises were 
made without comprehension of the responsibility being assumed, or they were made  
with full comprehension and without the character to keep them. The first is an indictment 
of capacity. The second is an indictment of character. Neither can be reconciled with the 
trust of public office. The mayor later dismissed the veto he did not issue as performative 
politics. But fidelity under pressure is not performance, it is character. The performance 
was the promise made to obtain power, then abandoned when power demanded courage. 
Manchester deserved conviction. It received choreography, and the spirit of evasion has 
poisoned our public debate. Question police spending, one is called anti-police; question 
school spending, one is called anti -child. Ask why another infusion of money will cure 
what decades of spending have not , and suddenly the citi zen, not the failure, is placed 
on trial. That is not an argument , it is an institution seeking refuge from accountability. I 
want safe streets.  I want officers in our neighborhoods. I want schools worthy of every 
child entrusted to them. It is precisely b ecause these things matter that the questions 
must be asked. If compensation alone will not fill police vacancies, what else is driving 
the crisis? If rising school budgets have not produced acceptable academic results, where 
is the reckoning? Where is the  reform? Have decisions made inside this chamber made 
Manchester harder to police, harder to teach in, harder to own property and harder to 
afford? In a republic public power must answer public scrutiny. The refusal to answer is 
the chasm that is now openi ng between City Hall and the citizenry. A government that 
resists scrutiny has forgotten the source of its authority. Public office is a trust, not a
August 4, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 5 of 62 
 
shield. The people are not subjects to be managed, taxed or ignored. They are sovereign 
citizens from whom  every ounce of governmental power is borrowed. This is now a 
struggle for the soul of Manchester. Will we become a city where promises are campaign 
instruments and institutions stand above examination and every failure becomes a claim 
upon the taxpayer? O r will we restore government discipline by truth, humbled by 
accountability and animated by reform? Trust cannot be commanded after it is broken. It 
must be earned through candor, repentance, reform, accountability, and, where 
necessary, new leadership. You overrode the tax cap. You did not override the people's 
memory. You did not erase the promise, and you did not extinguish the judgment that 
follows when a government breaks face with those it was elected to serve. 
 
Glenn Ouellette, 351 Chestnut Street: I'm going to come out with different topics tonight. 
Two topics. One is housing and parking. We seem to have in the city now where landlords 
who build apartments brand new from the buildings don't require to build one and a half 
parking spaces or cars per tenant. And now that I'm more into the center city, I find that 
every parking space is had, and when events are happening, multiple events at one time 
over the weekends, there is no place to park. None whatsoever. It is time or we'll have to 
pay the price and build a garage which we cannot afford to build, that we stop giving these 
waivers. These waivers do not help our city. They help an individual who's building 
something. And we need housing so bad that if they don't build it, somebody else will 
come. We need to do what's right for our city and stop waiving these things. The second 
issue is the state of New Hampshire , t he state legislature and the senators and the 
Executive Council and the governor. They need to respect the city of Manchester much 
more than they have been.  Do you remember when they created Boston Express? The 
state paid for those buses, and they paid for every one of the stations that were built to 
the point that Nashua has two bus stations that the state built. We had to repair ours for 
$250,000, and still they did not come. We are the biggest city north of Boston, and the 
buses have to park outside in rain or snow. Shame on us. We found the property where 
the Bank of America was, on the corner of Chestnut and the old Chestnut Road. It goes 
all the way around. There's plenty of parking. The state needs to be considering to buy 
that, to make that our bus station here in the city. We in the city of Manchester deserve 
to have a bus station. If you have to go to Londonderry and you don't hav e a car, you're 
not getting there. It's time for this board to write a letter to the appropriate people and to
August 4, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 6 of 62 
 
get us that building. It can be done  if you  people here on this board decide that it's 
important to the city. 
 
Rich Girard, 283 Orange Street: Not that long ago, an answer to questions from Aldermen 
Sapienza and Kantor, Police Chief Peter Marr essentially said he wasn't interested in 
entering into a 287 (g) agreement with ICE because the department was too busy to do 
immigration enforcement. He also  said the department asked about the immigration 
status of every person arrested, and that those found with I CE detainers were turned 
over. His answers to Alderman Kantor's request about whether or not the department 
turned known illegal aliens over to ICE after being arrested or convicted of crimes, clearly 
indicated that the department did not do that. In communications I had with the chief about 
a traffic enforcement article I published in October, he indicated that out of 3,525 arrests 
from the beginning of last year through the end of last September, they had turned over 
just four arrested individuals to I CE, one with a detainer, one after resisting arrest and 
discovering he'd been deported three times , and two from motor vehicle stops w here 
further investigation found deportation histories. I bring this up because about a week 
ago, a member of my TV show audience sent me an article from the Keene Sentinel about 
the police department in the tiny town of Troy, New Hampshire, population 2000 . Since 
the Troy Police Department entered into a 287(g) agreement with ICE in March of 2025, 
it has arrested 30 illegal aliens just from traffic enforcement efforts on Route 12. Their 
efforts to identify the drivers of the stopped vehicles uncovered their illegal status es, 
according to the article. Troy Police Chief David Ellis said that after pulling over a car for 
an alleged traffic violation, officers ask for identification from the driver and sometimes 
the passenger. Any immigration arrest would be made after the off icer checked with an 
ICE supervisor. If ICE wants them, then the Troy PD brings them right here to Manchester, 
where there's an I CE office, which seems to be the only time in position on that 
department. I'm bringing this to your attention, because in ligh t of the contracts given to 
the police unions, the cost of which still has not been fully disclosed , still waiting for that 
information, Mr. Mayor, there's been a lot of talk from members of this board about public 
safety. Your Honor, you've gone so far as to pat yourself on the back in social media ads 
for protecting public safety by granting these pay raises. Perhaps you'll be saying the 
same thing when the teachers’ unions say that higher pay equals better student 
outcomes, despite decades of proof that it doesn't, but I digress. If public safety is truly
August 4, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 7 of 62 
 
your concern , i t would seem to be a no brainer to direct the Manchester Police 
Department to enter into an agreement with I CE. There's no reason why someone here 
illegally shouldn't be turned over after they've been arrested for a crime, or any violation 
of law. Four illegal aliens turned over to I CE out of 3,525 arrests. Does that sound right 
to you? Let's face it, these are numbers that would make any sanctuary city proud. It's 
time Manchester stopped pretending it's not a sanctuary city, and start removing people 
who violate the law while already being here illegally. That will actually make our city safer 
and ultimately, our police less busy. 
 
Lisa Gravel, Ward 7: A lot has been made that the last time I appeared before this board, 
I told those of you that voted to override the tax cap to go to hell. Sorry , not sorry. I said 
what I said, and I stand by it. I despise you people. I am sure outside of city politics many 
of you are perfectly nice people. But I got to tell you, you suck as alderm en and mayor. 
Since I last spoke, I found out exactly just how much t hose portable classrooms at 
Southside cost: $28 million. I'm going to say that again : $28 million. That is real money 
that you have flushed right down the toilet. I was angry before, but now I am livid. I shudder 
to think what we are paying for this new ad dition. You are incompetent, irresponsible 
stewards of taxpayer money and it never ends. What you people have done is comparable 
to maxing out every one of your credit cards, then knocking on your neighbor's door and 
handing them the bill. It is easy to sp end so freely when someone else is picking up the 
tab, isn't it? I think you people are addicted to spending.  Now, I have heard through the 
grapevine that one of the authors of this reckless tax -cap-breaking budget thinks she 
deserves a promotion for mayor . Are you kidding me? What an absolute joke. It takes 
breathtaking arrogance to look at this budget and conclude it is a qualification for higher 
office. This would be like putting an arsonist in charge of the fire department. If she has 
any sense of humil ity, she will slink back to the life she had before public office and let 
someone else repair the damage her and her cohorts have created. If what I am saying 
tonight hurts, too bad. Trust me, what people at home are saying is a lot worse. I can't tell 
you the positive feedback I have received since the last meeting. So many people reached 
out to cheer me on. I got hugs, high fives, and a lot of atta girls. It gives me hope that 
perhaps the residents of this city are finally fed up enough to make some chang es and 
right this ship, because Manchester cannot take much more of the fiscal irresponsibility 
coming out of City Hall. And when you get your tax bill this December right in time for
August 4, 2026 BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN 
Page 8 of 62 
 
Christmas, and a ll the people sitting right there, people have to realiz e that we cannot 
keep electing the same people and expecting different results. If your alderman voted yes 
on the budget, they deserve to be kicked to the curb and hopefully the door won't hit them 
in the ass on their way out. 
 
Leonardo Rodrik, 1000 Elm Street: I am a resident of Manchester and a regular attendee 
of these meetings. This is my second meeting I've been to. I want to start by expressing 
my sincere gratitude. Thank you for listening to the voices of the people. Thank you for 
acting on the issue s we raised last time. And thank you for proving that when citizens 
speak up, their voices are heard. In June, the U.S. Attorney's Office announced the 
indictment of five men in the Homeland Security Task Force investigation. These 
individuals were running  a 30-month cross state drug trafficking conspiracy that 
specifically targeted Manchester and Seabrook, with more than three pounds  of 
methamphetamine and more than half a kilogram of fentanyl. That operation required 
undercover purchases, multiple agencie s, and federal coordination on homelessness. 
The new shelter at 200 Elm Street is now serving our elderly and disabled homeless 
population, and I'm proud to report that in its first two months of operation, there have 
been no arrests and no drug overdoses at this facility. Furthermore, the city has now 
housed all 47 veterans who were once without a home and helped 84 veterans overall
